what_its_for: This medication is a combination birth control pill (oral contraceptive) used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two female hormones — levonorgestrel (a progestin) and ethinyl estradiol (an estrogen) — that work together to stop ovulation (release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and thin the uterine lining. It may also be prescribed to help regulate periods, reduce menstrual cramps, or treat acne.
how_to_take: Take ONE pill by mouth every day, at the SAME TIME each day. Taking it at the same time helps it work best and reduces side effects like nausea. You can take it with or without food. Start your first pack on the first day of your period OR on the first Sunday after your period begins — follow your doctor's instructions. Follow the arrows on the pill pack and take pills in the correct order. Do not skip pills or take them out of order. Use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days if you are starting the pill for the first time.
dosing: Take 1 active (hormone) pill daily for 21 days, then take 1 inactive (reminder/placebo) pill daily for 7 days, or take no pill for 7 days — depending on your specific pill pack. Your period will usually come during the inactive pill or pill-free week. After finishing one pack, start a new pack the very next day — do not take a break between packs unless instructed. Never take more than 1 pill per day. Your doctor will determine the right formulation and dose for you.
missed_dose: Missing pills can make the medication less effective and increase your risk of pregnancy. Here is what to do: If you miss 1 active pill — take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next pill, take 2 pills that day. Use a backup method (like condoms) for 7 days. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 1 or 2 — take 2 pills for 2 days in a row to catch up, then continue as normal. Use a backup method for 7 days. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 3, OR if you miss 3 or more pills at any time — throw away the rest of the pack and start a new pack the next day (Sunday starters should keep taking pills until Sunday, then start a new pack). Use a backup method for 7 days. If you miss any inactive (reminder) pills, just throw them away and continue as scheduled. If you had unprotected sex and missed pills, contact your doctor or pharmacist — you may need emergency contraception.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep the pill pack in a dry place. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills that are past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Do not smoke while taking this medication — especially if you are over 35 years old. Smoking greatly increases the risk of serious heart and blood vessel problems such as blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice in large amounts, as it may affect how the medication works. Tell your doctor about all medications, vitamins, and supplements you take, because some drugs can make birth control pills less effective, including: certain antibiotics (like rifampin), seizure medications (like phenytoin or carbamazepine), HIV medications, St. John's Wort, and some antifungals. Avoid sitting or standing still for long periods of time, as birth control pills can slightly increase the risk of blood clots.
when_to_call_doctor: Seek EMERGENCY medical help (call 911) right away if you have: sudden severe chest pain or pressure, sudden shortness of breath, sudden severe headache unlike any you have had before, sudden vision changes or vision loss, sudden numbness or weakness on one side of the body, coughing up blood, severe leg pain or swelling in one leg, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Call your doctor as soon as possible if you notice: unusual vaginal bleeding, missed periods (especially if you have skipped pills), breast lumps or unusual breast changes, severe stomach pain or cramping, mood changes or signs of depression, worsening migraines or new migraines, high blood pressure, skin rash, or any new or concerning symptoms. Also call your doctor before stopping the pill if you plan to become pregnant or are having surgery.
when_it_works: Birth control pills are most effective when taken correctly every day. If you use them perfectly (same time every day, no missed pills), they are about 99% effective at preventing pregnancy. With typical use (occasional missed pills or timing errors), they are about 91% effective. Protection begins right away if you start on the first day of your period. If you start on another day, use backup birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days. The pill does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) — use condoms to reduce your STI risk.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking this pill, stop taking it and call your doctor. BREASTFEEDING: This medication may reduce milk supply. Talk to your doctor before using this pill while breastfeeding. Progestin-only pills are often preferred while nursing. TEENAGERS: This medication is generally safe for teens who have already started their periods. OLDER ADULTS (over 35): Women over 35 who smoke should NOT use this medication due to high risk of blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. Women over 35 who do not smoke may use it with their doctor's approval. LIVER DISEASE: Do not use if you have liver disease or tumors. HISTORY OF BLOOD CLOTS, STROKE, OR HEART ATTACK: This medication should generally NOT be used if you have had a blood clot, stroke, or heart attack. MIGRAINE WITH AURA: Women who have migraines with aura (visual disturbances before headache) should avoid this medication due to increased stroke risk. Always share your full medical history with your doctor before starting this medication.
